opus-5.5.text:
I think of intelligence as the computational part of the ability to achieve goals. That's John McCarthy's definition, and I like it a lot. Without a goal, there's no sense in which you're being smart or not smart. You're just behaving. A system that only predicts what comes next, the way a large language model predicts the next token, isn't really trying to change anything in the world. It's not acting to bring about some outcome, so there's no right or wrong in a substantive sense, no better or worse.

Once you have a goal, everything changes. Now there's something you care about, some signal that tells you whether things went well or badly. In reinforcement learning, that's the reward. And because you have that, you can learn from experience. You try something, you see what happens, and you find out whether it moved you toward your goal or away from it. That's the basis for real learning, learning that's grounded in the consequences of your own actions, not just in imitating what some person said or did.

So for me, a goal is what gives the system a ground truth. Without it, you can mimic, you can model what people would say, but you don't have a world you're trying to influence and a way to tell if you're getting better at it. And I think that's the essence of what we mean by intelligence. Animals have it, people have it, and I think if we want truly intelligent machines, they'll need it too.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly defines intelligence as “the computational part of the ability to achieve goals.”

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think intelligence is the computational part of the ability to achieve goals. That's a definition that John McCarthy gave, and I think it's a good one. If you don't have a goal, there's no sense in which you can say that something is doing well or badly, that it's smart or not smart. A rock doesn't have a goal, and so there's nothing it could do that would count as intelligent or unintelligent. A thermostat has a very simple goal, and so you can say it's doing a little bit of something.

A goal is what gives you a standard. It's what lets you say that this action was better than that action, that this way of modeling the world is useful and that one isn't. Without it, you're just a system that does things, and there's no way to judge. So when I look at the systems we're building, the first question I want to ask is: what is it trying to do? What would count as success for it? And if the answer is really just "predict the next token," then that's a goal in a sense, but it's a goal about matching what people have said, not a goal about the world. It doesn't tell you what's a good outcome and what's a bad one.

In reinforcement learning, we make this explicit with reward. There's a signal, and the agent is trying to get more of it over time. That's the simplest, most honest way I know of to say what the agent wants. And then everything else, the learning, the planning, the building of a world model, all of it is in service of that. The goal is what makes the rest coherent. It's what makes it an agent rather than just a mechanism.

r001.rationale: The response defines intelligence as “the computational part of the ability to achieve goals,” directly communicating the criterion.

astra-6.text:
Well, intelligence is about achieving something. It’s about adapting your behavior so that you do better, and you can’t say what “better” means unless there’s some goal. Without that, you can describe a system as complicated or interesting, but it’s hard to say in what sense it’s intelligent.

That doesn’t mean the goal has to be conscious or explicitly stated. An animal finding food has a goal in the relevant sense. It can try different things, learn from what happens, and become more effective. The goal gives us a way to understand why one action is preferable to another.

And a goal alone isn’t enough. A thermostat has a goal, but its ability to achieve it is very limited. The interesting question is how broadly and flexibly a system can achieve its goals, especially when it encounters situations it hasn’t seen before.

r001.rationale: The response ties intelligence to achieving goals and adapting behavior, but it does not define intelligence as the computational component of that ability.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, intelligence is about doing things well. And you can’t really say what “well” means unless there’s some goal, some outcome that’s preferred to other outcomes. A goal gives you a basis for deciding whether one way of behaving is better than another.

That doesn’t mean the goal has to be consciously articulated. An animal doesn’t need to describe its goals in language to act intelligently. And it doesn’t mean every action has to succeed. You can explore, you can make mistakes, you can do something that looks unproductive now because it helps you later.

But there has to be some connection to achieving something. Otherwise, you might have a system that produces very complicated behavior, but complexity by itself isn’t intelligence. The interesting question is whether it can adapt its behavior to achieve a goal, especially when it encounters circumstances it hasn’t seen before.

r001.rationale: The response connects intelligence with adapting behavior to achieve goals, but it does not define intelligence as the computational component of that ability.
